extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV/comedy fans, and those researching the Roast Battle television format
extracted.subtask_description: Documentation of the UK television series Roast Battle: its concept, format, production and reception — useful for producers, researchers, or performers studying the show's structure and standards. Focuses on how battles are staged, judged, produced and regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winner determination
rubrics_metrics.description: "The winner of each battle is determined by a panel of judges, including Carr."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges decide who wins each head-to-head roast battle; episode listings mark winners in bold. The panel composition has varied across series (see Judges entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show format — comedians facing each other in roast battles
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show ... features comedians facing each other in roast battles."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format is head-to-head insult/roast exchanges between two comedians, adapted from the American Jeff Ross Presents Roast Battle and the live Comedy Store show. Implies a structured competitive exchange rather than solo sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host and referee roles
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show is hosted by Jimmy Carr and Moses acts as the announcer and the referee of each battle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Host presents and participates in the show; an announcer/referee manages turn-taking and enforces the live/rules aspects of each battle. These roles shape pacing and adjudication though judges determine winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges: composition and guest-judge practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Page lists regular and guest judges (e.g., Katherine Ryan, Russell Brand, Jonathan Ross) and notes that series 4 featured Ryan alongside a different guest judge each episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge panels vary by series and episode; guest judges are commonly used (examples: Richard Ayoade, Big Narstie, Sara Pascoe, Noel Fielding, Joe Lycett). The choice of judges is a production decision that affects evaluation and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre and tonal standard — roast/insult comedy, satire, stand-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Genre listing: "Comedy; Satire; Stand-up comedy" and the article repeatedly references 'roast' and 'insult comedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content is expected to be roast/insult-driven and satirical in tone; producers and performers operate within that comedic tradition while balancing broadcast rules and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and source-format compliance (based on live show)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The American series is based on a live show created by Moses and fellow comedian Rell Battle that runs at The Comedy Store in Los Angeles in the comedy club's Belly Room."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The television format is an adaptation of an established live competition; production and performance conventions (timing, referee role, head-to-head structure) reflect the live show's rules and ethos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording venue and production partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: "The show is recorded at the Electric Brixton nightclub in London and is co-produced by James Corden’s production company Fulwell 73 and Carr's production company Ideasatron."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies production/location requirements for the UK series; venue and production companies are part of the series' production standard and affect staging, audience size and show presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure and series formatting (battles per episode, episode counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episode tables show typically two battles per episode; transcriptions include series and episode counts (e.g., Series 1: 6 episodes; Series 2: 5; Series 4: 5 episodes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard episode structure is multiple head-to-head battles (commonly two) per episode; series lengths and special episodes (e.g., Christmas special, play-off, final) are part of programming format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast standards and regulatory risk (Ofcom complaint)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In December 2018, a complaint was upheld by Ofcom after a trailer for the programme featured an anti-Semitic joke delivered by Jimmy Carr..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though roast/insult comedy pushes boundaries, broadcasters and producers must comply with regulatory standards (e.g., avoid discriminatory/anti‑religious content that breaches rules). The Ofcom ruling is an example of enforced limits on acceptable content for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception metric — ratings success as a success indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: "Roast Battle became Comedy Central's highest-rated UK commission."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience ratings are used as a measure of the show's success and viability; critical reception and regulatory outcomes (e.g., complaints) also affect overall reception and reputation.
